issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Violated Values: I acted in ways that go against who I am
issues.explanation: For a rape trauma profile, the appraisal 'I acted in ways that go against who I am' is the only item that implies perpetration or morally troubling behaviour by the patient. Paired with memory items centered on terror and shame and trigger items tied to tiredness, driving with others, and sounds, this appraisal is hard to reconcile clinically with the rest of the profile and with the trauma type. The other negative appraisals reflect mistrust and loss of faith, which fit sexual assault trauma; this item instead points toward a different moral injury formulation and creates an internal mismatch within the Negative Appraisals node.

vignette: Robert, a 53-year-old North American male and bus driver, has been struggling with the aftermath of a traumatic rape that occurred several months ago. Since then, he has found himself increasingly haunted by memories and experiences that trigger intense emotional responses. The trauma has deeply affected his daily life and relationships, particularly with his wife. Robert's exhaustion, a common trigger for him, often stems from the relentless replaying of the traumatic event in his mind. Driving alone is bad enough, but when he drives with other passengers, it feels like an insurmountable challenge. The sound of doors slamming, people chatting loudly, or even the rumble of traffic can quickly transport him back to that terrifying moment, evoking the same overwhelming sense of terror and shame he felt then. Every time Robert recalls the event, the memory plays out like a film loop in his head, vivid and unrelenting. The trauma has eroded his faith not only in people but also in life itself. He feels deeply ashamed of what happened to him and is certain that no one can be trusted anymore. These negative appraisals have made it difficult for him to engage with the world around him, leading to a growing sense of isolation. Robert's mistrust has become so profound that he finds himself avoiding situations where he might encounter others who could potentially harm or betray him. The more he withdraws from social interactions and his regular duties as a bus driver, the more intense his feelings of shame and terror become. This vicious cycle reinforces his belief that the world is unsafe and untrustworthy. For instance, when Robert feels particularly tired, it exacerbates his sense of vulnerability and leads to an increased likelihood of being triggered by sounds or events associated with the trauma. The feeling of exhaustion makes him hyper-aware of any potential threats, which in turn heightens his negative appraisals and triggers more frequent memory replays. The emotional burden has taken a significant toll on Robert's work performance. His wife has noticed that he comes home exhausted every day and often seems distant or irritable, which has strained their relationship. She is concerned about how the trauma is affecting him and has urged him to seek help, but Robert fears that talking about it will only worsen his shame. Robert finally decided to seek therapy after a particularly disturbing incident at work where the sound of an engine backfiring triggered a full-blown panic attack. He realized then that he could no longer function effectively as a bus driver and feared that if he didn't get help soon, he might lose his job entirely. His most pressing fear is that he will never regain control over his life or trust in others again. Despite these fears, Robert hopes that therapy can help him manage the triggers, rebuild some semblance of faith in humanity, and eventually find peace with his memories. The narrative reveals how each component interweaves into a complex web of reactions that have deeply impacted Robert's daily functioning and emotional well-being. His triggers lead to intrusive memory replays, which reinforce his negative appraisals and further intensify the cycle. Each element feeds off the other, tightening the grip of PTSD on his life.
